meta.method_md:
## What this tree is

One primary hierarchy answers **what work the computer is being used for**, from the root down to small task classes of about 20 concrete tasks each. Separate labels on every task (the facets) answer **where and how**: operating system, interface (GUI, terminal, API), interaction primitives, work product, and whether the task really needs a GUI.

"Computer use" here is deliberately broad: desktop GUI apps, browsers, phones, terminals and coding, data and infrastructure work, and physical systems controlled through software (robots, PLCs, printers, drones).

## Why the levels are not OS × app

- **OS × app explodes and duplicates.** Five operating systems times thousands of applications yields a list, not a hierarchy, and the same work ("color-grade a clip") appears under Premiere, Resolve and Final Cut on two systems.
- **Apps change; work persists.** O*NET separates work activities from tools for this reason, and ALE organizes 55 subdomains by occupation (O*NET / SOC 2018), not by software. Inheriting that keeps this tree aligned with ALE.
- **Skill transfers along work, not along vendors.** Keying is keying in After Effects or Nuke. Grouping by work makes per-branch scores mean something.
- OS and app remain fully filterable: they are facets on every task, so "all macOS + Windows tasks in Creative" is one click.

## Levels

- **L1 Realm** is the sphere of activity. Fifteen realms cover platform operations, software, data, information work, business operations, creative media, engineering, science, health, law and public services, communication, everyday life, games, finance, and education/knowledge services.
- **L2 Domain** is a discipline or function, aligned to ALE subdomains and O*NET/SOC families wherever one exists.
- **L3 Workflow family** is a recurring end-to-end workflow. It is defined by its goal, its work product and how the result is judged; an app name or input size alone never defines a family (the FrontierCUA family rule).
- **L4 Task class** is the leaf. It holds tasks that share setup style, verification template and core skill, so that about 20 instances can vary inputs, apps, OS and difficulty without changing what is measured. **Leaf test:** if one verifier template cannot grade all of them, split; if two leaves share a template and a skill, merge.

## Placement rules

1. **Place by the purpose of the deliverable** (whose job is it?). A quarterly chart built in Excel goes to *Information & Document Work › Spreadsheets*; closing the month in QuickBooks goes to *Finance › Accounting*.
2. **Professional and personal versions split only when the workflow differs.** Buying as a consumer (Everyday Life) and procurement (Business) are separate; email triage is one place (Communication).
3. **Cross-cutting skills are facets, not branches.** Search, file handling, drag, real-time control and accessibility mode are facets. They become branches only when they are the goal itself, as in OS file management or building an automation.
4. **Surfaces are facets.** TV, car, XR and screen-reader interfaces are values of the surface facet; their tasks live where their purpose puts them.
5. **Single parent.** Every node has one parent; related nodes elsewhere are mentioned in the definition text rather than duplicated.

## CUA need: does this task need a GUI?

Every task carries two labels on the same five-level scale:

- **`need`** is the GUI need **as designed**, in the task's own environment. Its verifier may withhold the terminal or audit for scripted bypasses; the validator requires this of every GUI-essential and GUI-only task. This label says how the task will be run and graded.
- **`need_open`** is the GUI need of the work itself **with ordinary access** (Step 0 below). It is a blind label: three raters (one Claude, two Codex) per task, majority rule (Evaluation → Round 10). It says whether a task is a good test of computer use at all. 不适合 CLI 但适合 CUA means `need_open` is GUI-essential or GUI-only.

The two agree on 42% of tasks. GUI share is 62% as designed and 58% with ordinary access; 1,316 tasks are GUI tasks only because of their environment. The site's GUI-need switch shows every view either way.

The five levels:

- **API-sufficient:** a documented API, SDK or MCP server does the whole task. It is not a CUA task unless the GUI itself is under test.
- **CLI-sufficient:** a terminal plus files does it end to end with standard tools. It belongs to ALE-CLI, or serves as the control half of a GUI/CLI pair.
- **Hybrid:** the expert solution splits into a real GUI part and a substantial scripted part. It tests tool switching.
- **GUI-essential:** a script route exists in principle (bpy, ExtendScript, UNO), but success depends on the visual loop: continuous or spatial manipulation, perceptual judgment, or interactive tools.
- **GUI-only:** there is no practical programmatic route. The state lives only behind the GUI (closed app, no API, SAP GUI, Citrix or remote desktop, legacy terminal).

**How to decide: rubric v4.** It replaced the earlier definitions plus tie-breaks after round 6 of the blind test. On 171 fresh tasks it raised six-rater agreement from κ 0.755 to 0.845 and Claude–Codex agreement from 80% to 90% (Evaluation → Round 6), and it held on 156 more (κ 0.875, round 8). Go through the steps in order and stop at the first that decides.

0. **Fix the environment and the target.** Assume ordinary user access: a desktop with the apps the task names, a terminal, and common open-source tools; for phone tasks, a computer connected over adb. Use only the accounts and keys the task gives. Judge the checked end state, not the route the task suggests: "in GIMP" does not change the label unless the checked state lives inside that app.
1. **Websites.** A task done on a website or web app is GUI-essential. It is API-sufficient only if the task mentions an API, token, SDK or MCP server for the site, and CLI-sufficient only if the task gives a direct link to a data file. A browser's own settings and extensions are desktop-app state.
2. **A view left on screen** (a window, dialog or tab left open, a form filled but not saved, media playing, an item selected) is GUI-only, unless one documented command opens exactly that view; then it is CLI-sufficient.
3. **Reading the screen.** A task that points at on-screen state no file records ("this page", "where my cursor is", "the current frame") is GUI-essential.
4. **A program route.** API-sufficient if a documented API does the whole task. CLI-sufficient if the terminal and files do it end to end without needing to look at the result.
   - Routes that count: standard tools; libraries that edit a format faithfully (python-docx, openpyxl, python-pptx, ffmpeg, ImageMagick); vendor-documented config files, `defaults` keys, policies and options; an app's own scripting interface (AppleScript dictionary, COM, UNO, Blender Python); documented adb system commands.
   - Routes that do not count: UI scripting that clicks or types (System Events, xdotool, AutoHotkey, pyautogui, `adb shell input`); hand-editing an app's internal files or databases; undocumented keys; privacy-protected (TCC) stores.
   - Geometry computed from the file (positions, sizes, alignment) is not visual judgment.
   - Documents: CLI-sufficient if a library edits the format faithfully; GUI-essential if the result depends on rendering or needs app-only features (pivot tables, SmartArt, themes, tracked changes).
5. **The GUI is needed.**
   - **Hybrid:** a real GUI part plus a substantial scripted part (bulk data, many files, code). A single command beside a GUI job is not Hybrid.
   - **GUI-essential:** the app has a programmatic route, but this task needs the visual loop or a UI-only setting.
   - **GUI-only:** the app or system offers no programmatic route at all.

**Several parts:** label each part and take the most GUI-demanding, unless Hybrid applies. **Still torn between two adjacent labels:** choose the one needing less GUI; the GUI label has to be earned.

**ALE-CUA should draw from GUI-only and GUI-essential**, use Hybrid to test tool switching, and use CLI- and API-sufficient tasks as controls. The Facets view shows this mix for every branch.

## Why CUA and not just coding: evidence so far

- **Drag is the bottleneck, not reasoning.** The same Scratch tasks score 14.46% when blocks must be dragged versus 78.31% through a semantic API, and every model scored 0% on The Incredible Machine in VideoGameBench.
- **API-only benchmarks saturate; GUI ones do not.** WorkBench rose from 43% to 98% in two years, while WorkArena++ L3 is at 0%, multi-app WindowsWorld is under 21%, and SpreadsheetBench v2 is at 34.9%.
- **The API route has holes exactly where professionals work.** openpyxl cannot create pivot tables; python-pptx cannot author SmartArt or apply themes; SAP GUI, Citrix and 3270 terminals expose no API at all, which is why RPA vendors exist.
- **Real-time control is a separate difficulty.** VideoGameBench scores 0.48% when the game runs live versus 1.6% when it pauses for the model.
- **Hidden APIs make tasks invalid.** In one public agent experiment a model failed to make a chess move through the Lichess UI for 28 sessions, then succeeded at once through the API. GUI tasks must block shortcut APIs, or they silently stop measuring CUA.

## Task records

Each task carries an ID, a title, a concrete prompt with inputs and the expected output, operating systems, surface, apps, CUA need, interaction primitives, work product, a verification method, partial-credit milestones and an estimated difficulty from 1 to 5. Tasks are **proposals**: they are written to the FrontierCUA quality bar (well defined, low expected pass rate, deterministic or rubric-checkable, partial credit for training), but none has been implemented or run yet, and difficulty is an estimate, not a measured pass rate.

## How it was built

1. **Discovery: 14 parallel research lanes** covered:
   - professional-work benchmarks and ALE
   - occupational standards (O*NET 31.0, SOC 2018, ISCO-08, BLS employment, Anthropic Economic Index)
   - desktop, web, mobile and terminal benchmarks
   - creative, engineering, science, health, law and business software
   - OS and consumer computing
   - taxonomy theory and vendor demand

   Together they logged **1,504 lookups**: 279 web-search calls, some refused by the session's 200-search cap, plus 1,204 direct reads of primary pages, papers, repositories and official data files. That produced **859 distinct source URLs**, **596 benchmark entries** before de-duplication, and **749 candidate task classes with 2,801 example tasks**. Per-lane files with every query and source are in `research/cua-lineage/phase1/`.
2. **Synthesis:** I merged the candidates into the four levels under the rules above. All 55 ALE subdomains are placed. Benchmarks were de-duplicated and mapped onto the task classes their tasks fall into.
3. **Task writing:** 20 tasks per task class, written against the class definition and facets by parallel writers, each file checked by a schema validator.
4. **Independent verification, in rounds.** A separate checker built a 13-criterion acceptance manifest and judged the artifacts directly, not the writers' reports.
   - **Round 1: FAIL** (7 pass).
     - 22 of 749 candidates were unplaced.
     - 11 classes were labelled GUI-heavy but were mostly Hybrid.
     - Many GUI tasks did not say how shortcuts are blocked, and 914 partial-credit lists were malformed.
     - 3 tasks touched live channels.

     Fixes: 18 classes were added and 11 defaults relabelled honestly. Both rules became validator checks, every file was repaired, and the live-channel tasks moved to test channels.
   - **Round 2: FAIL** (11 pass).
     - 2 sibling live-channel tasks remained.
     - New classes had no benchmark mapping.
     - About 12 GUI tasks passed the keyword check by accident.
     - 2 near-duplicates had appeared.

     Fixes: a full-tree safety sweep moved every state-changing task on a real platform to a test account, store or channel. The new classes were mapped, and the remaining 150 white-space classes are listed in `gen/white_space.json`. A semantic review covered 156 suspect tasks, a class was added for proactive act/ask/stay-silent judgment, and the duplicates were rewritten.
   - **Round 3: PARTIAL** (12 pass, 0 fail). All 749 candidates are resolved (748 placed, 1 scoped out), and safety has 0 violations.
     - The partial criterion is benchmark coverage: a missing white-space entry, and lane-cited benchmarks not yet mapped for 9 classes.
     - Within-threshold cleanups remained: 26 grading sentences, 7 test-context wordings and 4 near-duplicate pairs.

     Fixes: all of these were applied.
   - **Rounds 4–5: PARTIAL** (12 pass, 0 fail), still on benchmark coverage only.
     - Successive scans found white-space classes whose lane-cited benchmarks (ALE, Terminal-Bench 2.0, OSWorld, VideoGameBench, ScienceBoard and others) actually contain tasks of that kind. Round 5 found 18 that an earlier scan had missed by skipping short benchmark names.
     - One extra mapping was judged unsupported and removed.

     Result: benchmarks now touch **317 of 430 classes (73.7%)**. The remaining **113** are documented white space, where no public benchmark was found.

   Files: `gen/acceptance_manifest.json`, `gen/acceptance_results.json`, `gen/candidate_coverage.json`, `gen/scope_decisions.json`, `gen/white_space.json`.

5. **Blind tests, ten rounds.** For each scheme, three independent raters (six from two model families in rounds 5–8) placed real held-out tasks into it. Every round used tasks not seen before, from OSWorld (Ubuntu and Windows), WebArena, ALE, AndroidWorld and macOSWorld. The schemes compared were this tree, ALE's 55 subdomains, and FrontierCUA's earlier D01–D10 scheme.
   - **Coverage:** 0 of 342 unseen tasks in rounds 2–4 were unplaceable in this tree. ALE could not place 54–61% of everyday or macOS tasks.
   - **Clarity:** agreement on the exact task class held at κ 0.94 across 429–430 classes. At matched coarseness (13 realms vs 10 domains), this tree is at least as clear as D01–D10 (κ 0.98 vs 0.95).
   - **GUI need:** after tie-break rules and a macOS scripting rule, agreement on the GUI-need label reached κ 0.90 on fresh macOS tasks.
   - **Cross-model check:** three Codex (GPT) raters reproduced the placements. 88% of majority task-class labels match the Claude raters' (pooled κ 0.87). The GUI-need label was the least portable judgment (71% cross-model agreement), because it depends on what tool access the environment grants.
   - **Rubric v4 (round 6):** a pre-registered test on 171 fresh tasks compared the old and new GUI-need rubrics with six raters each. v4 raised agreement from κ 0.755 to 0.845 (+0.09, 95% CI +0.02 to +0.15) and Claude–Codex agreement from 80% to 90%.
   - **Definitions (round 7):** sixteen definitions broadened from earlier partial-fit notes raised exact fits on the same fresh tasks from 87.4% to 89.5% (+2.1 points, CI +0.3 to +4.3) without lowering agreement. 0 of 513 unseen tasks have been unplaceable since round 1.
   - **Own tasks (rounds 9–10):** blind raters put 88% of a 208-task sample of the tree's own tasks back in their exact class. Their GUI-need labels showed that many stored labels described an environment with routes withheld, not the work, so every task now also carries a blind `need_open`.
   - **Replication (round 8):** on 156 more fresh tasks v4 held (κ 0.875, 91% cross-model). A further refinement, v4.1, failed its pre-registered non-inferiority test and was not adopted.

   Details are on the Evaluation tab.

## Limits

- The web-search budget is shared across the session (200 searches); lanes therefore read many primary pages directly. The real counts are on the Sources list and in the research files, not estimates.
- Benchmark mappings place a benchmark where its tasks fall; they do not imply the benchmark covers that whole branch.
- The tree is versioned and meant to change: use the per-node feedback box and export the comments.

## Version 1.1: fifteen realms

Financial work and education/knowledge services now have independent realms. Nine existing domains (28 task classes, 560 proposals) move out of the previous Business, Law/Public Sector/Education and Everyday Life realms. The tree still contains 120 domains, 143 workflow families, 430 task classes and 8,600 proposals. This is a grouping revision, not new task collection.

Task IDs and original task evidence remain unchanged. A published node alias table resolves earlier class IDs and shared links to current addresses; local feedback is carried forward with its original node ID recorded. The base skeleton and task files remain preserved, and `realm-layout.json` records the build-time migration.

Earlier evaluation studies and occupational weights belong to the 13-realm structure. No new evaluation or weight estimation is claimed for the 15-realm revision. Digital employees remain a role and operating-model lens across the work taxonomy.
